# Principles of transgender health care

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Urologic surgery > Principles of transgender health care*

[Original Article Link](/library/L70wmh)

---

## Summary

<u>Transgender</u> people have a <u>gender identity</u> that differs from the <u>sex assigned at birth</u> and sometimes choose to undergo <u>hormone</u> therapy and/or <u>surgery</u> to align their physical appearance and <u>gender identity</u>. Often, <u>transgender</u> individuals face social and institutional discrimination and stigmatization that affect their quality of life, including experiences with the <u>health system</u> and access to care. Clinicians should be aware of these issues and ensure a welcoming environment that allows for patients to provide the necessary information to address their health needs. <u>Transgender</u> patients present with the same spectrum of health problems and needs as <u>cisgender</u> patients, and the majority of presentations will be unrelated to <u>gender identity</u>. <u>Hormone</u> therapy and <u>surgery</u> are typically overseen by specialist centers; however, some patients may subsequently present to their primary care physician or local hospital with treatment side effects and complications, including long-term changes to physiology (e.g., secondary to <u>gonadectomy</u> and <u>gender-affirming hormone therapy</u>) that can increase the risk of certain diseases. <u>Transgender</u> people also face unique challenges in managing <u>fertility</u>, <u>contraception</u>, and <u>pregnancy</u>.




See also “<u>Sexuality and sexual medicine</u>” and “<u>Gender dysphoria</u>.”
